client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to get my head straight. Every time I sit down to study, I end up staring at the wall or thinking about him, and I feel this heavy weight in my chest that won't go away. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me actually open a textbook, but I figured I'd try something.
therapist: It means a lot that you reached out, even when part of you wasn't sure it would help — that took courage, especially when you're carrying so much right now. Losing your grandfather while facing exams is a genuinely heavy combination, and that weight in your chest makes complete sense; grief doesn't pause for deadlines. I'd love to understand a little more — when you sit down to study and your mind drifts to him, what kinds of thoughts tend to come up for you?

client: It's mostly guilt, honestly. Like, I'll be trying to memorize something for my biology exam and then I'll suddenly think, "How can I even care about this right now?" and then I feel terrible for not studying harder, but also terrible for studying at all. It's like I can't do anything right — I'm failing him by moving on, and failing myself by not moving on.
therapist: That painful double-bind you're describing — feeling wrong no matter which direction you turn — sounds absolutely exhausting, like you're trapped between two impossible standards. It's such a common but cruel trick grief plays on us, making us believe that caring about our own life somehow means we care less about the person we lost. I'm curious — do you think your grandfather would actually see you sitting down to study as a betrayal of him, or is that a story the grief is telling you right now?

client: I mean... honestly, no, he probably wouldn't see it that way. He was always pushing me to do well in school, that was actually really important to him. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it when I sit down to open my textbook are two completely different things — it's like the guilt just doesn't care about logic.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really important — there's a part of you that *knows* studying would actually honor him, and that's not a small thing. You're right that insight and feeling don't always move at the same speed, and that gap can be frustrating, but in CBT we can actually use that knowledge as a gentle anchor when the guilt flares up — almost like a reminder you can return to in those moments. When the guilt hits at your desk, what do you think it would feel like to quietly say to yourself, "doing this *is* how I carry him with me"?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that would work, but honestly it feels a little too neat, like a phrase I'd be forcing myself to say while not really feeling it. When the guilt hits it's not like a gentle wave I can just redirect with a few words — it's more like this sudden heaviness that kind of shuts everything down. I'm worried it would just feel hollow, like I'm lying to myself instead of actually grieving him.
therapist: That's really honest feedback, and you're right to push back on that — a phrase that doesn't match what you're actually feeling inside can end up feeling dismissive of your own grief rather than helpful. What you're describing, that sudden heaviness that shuts everything down, sounds less like a thought you can reframe in the moment and more like something your body and heart need space to actually move through first. I'm wondering — when that heaviness arrives, do you ever allow yourself to just pause and feel it for a few minutes, rather than either forcing yourself to study through it or feeling guilty for stopping?

client: Honestly, I don't really let myself do that — pause and just feel it. It seems like every time I try, I end up spiraling into thinking about how much time I'm wasting or how far behind I'm falling, and then the guilt just piles on top of the grief and it gets worse. I guess I'm not sure I trust myself to come back out of it if I actually let myself go there.
therapist: That fear of being swallowed whole by the grief if you let yourself feel it — that's such an understandable place to be, and it makes a lot of sense that you've been keeping a lid on it to stay functional. What's actually happening though is that the effort of holding it back is likely taking up the very energy you need for studying, creating that exhausting loop you're stuck in. I'm curious — has there ever been a time in your life when you let yourself feel something difficult and actually did find your way back out the other side?

client: I mean... yeah, there was a time in high school when my dog died and I cried for like two days straight, and eventually I did feel better. But this feels so much bigger than that — losing my dad isn't something you just cry out and move on from. I guess I'm scared that if I start, it won't be like that, it'll just be endless and I'll completely fall apart right before my exams.
therapist: You actually just gave yourself some really meaningful evidence — a part of you already knows you have the capacity to move through grief and come back, even if this loss feels on a completely different scale. The fear that it will be "endless" is grief talking, trying to protect you, but feelings — even the biggest ones — do move when we give them room, they don't stay at their peak forever. I'm wondering, what would it look like to give yourself a small, bounded space to feel this — say, ten or fifteen minutes with permission to grieve, but also with a gentle agreement with yourself that you'll return — rather than an all-or-nothing plunge?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets the logic of it — like, okay, set a timer, let yourself cry, then come back to solid ground. But honestly, the idea of deliberately opening that door, even for just fifteen minutes, feels terrifying, like I'd be inviting something in that I can't control. What if I sit down to grieve and I just... can't stop, even with the agreement I made with myself?
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and I want to name something important — the fact that you're scared of your own grief doesn't mean the grief is unmanageable, it means you haven't yet had a safe enough experience to trust that you can survive it. You don't have to take that leap alone or all at once, and part of what therapy can offer is being a kind of "spotter" while you test how much weight you can actually hold. What do you think would need to feel true, or be in place, for you to feel even slightly safer about taking that small step toward your grief?

client: I think what you said about not having had a safe enough experience... that actually landed differently than I expected. Like, it's not that I'm broken or weak, it's that I genuinely haven't had proof yet that I can get through it without falling apart completely. But I guess what I'd need is some kind of guarantee that I won't just completely shut down or lose control, and I know you can't actually give me that, which is what makes it so hard to even try.
therapist: You're showing real clarity right now — you've named exactly what you need and also why it feels out of reach, and that kind of self-awareness is actually a strength, not a small thing. You're right that I can't give you a guarantee, but I want to gently offer this: the fact that you're here, articulating all of this so honestly, is itself evidence that you don't completely fall apart under pressure — you reach out, you reflect, you keep going. What if the proof you're looking for isn't something I can hand you, but something you've actually already started building, right here in this conversation?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it also feels a little too neat, you know? Like, showing up to therapy and talking about my problems isn't the same as actually handling things when I'm alone at 2am and the anxiety is just crushing me. I guess I'm worried that what I can do in here doesn't translate to out there, where everything feels so much harder and there's no one to catch me if I spiral.
therapist: That distinction you're drawing is real and important — there *is* a difference between insight in a safe conversation and being alone at 2am when everything feels like it's closing in, and it would be dishonest of me to pretend otherwise. But I'd gently ask you to notice something: at 2am, you're not starting from zero anymore — you're starting with everything you've already uncovered here, including the knowledge that your grief isn't weakness, and that you've survived hard things before. What does 2am actually look like for you right now — what's happening in those moments, and what have you been doing to get through them?

client: Honestly, 2am looks like me lying in bed scrolling through old text conversations with my brother, just reading them over and over like I'm trying to find something I missed. The apartment feels so quiet it's almost loud, if that makes any sense, and I start thinking about how he was the one person I could call at any hour and now that's just... gone. I usually end up falling asleep with the TV on because I can't stand the silence, which I know isn't really "getting through it" so much as just waiting for morning.
therapist: What you just described — the quiet that feels almost loud, searching through those messages like there's something left to find — that's such a tender and human picture of grief, and it makes complete sense that you're drawn to those conversations when everything feels so still and empty. I want to gently reflect something back to you: you've been describing losing your grandfather throughout our conversation, but just now you said "he was the one person I could call at any hour" — I want to make sure I'm understanding, are you also grieving your brother, or is your brother still here but this loss has changed something between you two as well?
